    Home/Learn/What “research use only” means on a peptide label

    What “research use only” means on a peptide label.

    Peptide Chooser editorial team. Checked 30 Oct 2026.

    Short answer

    "Research use only" is wording the seller puts on its own label. It is not an FDA approval and says nothing about what is in the vial. The FDA looks at how a product is sold: in its letters it says that when a website shows the product is meant for people, the label does not change that.1

    What does the label say?

    Research-use shops label their vials with words such as "research use only", "for laboratory use" or "not for human consumption". The shop writes these words itself; no regulator gives or checks them.

    An approved medicine is different: its maker sent the FDA trial data and the FDA found the benefits outweigh the known risks for the people it is meant for.2 A research-use vial has been through none of that.

    What does the FDA say about it?

    The FDA looks at what a product is meant for, from all of the seller's words and pages, not only the label. In an August 2026 letter to a peptide shop, it said that despite the shop's "for laboratory, research, and analytical use" wording, its website showed the products were meant as drugs for people. The letter pointed to a "peptide calculator" sold alongside mixing water.1

    The FDA has also warned companies selling GLP-1 drugs labeled "for research purposes" or "not for human consumption" that were in fact sold to people with dosing instructions, and it urges people not to buy them.3

    What do the shops' own pages say?

    We show how many shops have terms pages once our crawler has read them.

    A shop's terms page often repeats the research-only wording and asks the buyer to agree that the product is not for people. Having the page says nothing about what it promises; read the refund part before you trust it.

    Why do shops use the label?

    A product sold as a medicine for people needs FDA approval before it is sold.2 The research-only label is the shop's way of saying its vial is not a medicine. The FDA's letters show it does not accept that when the rest of the site, such as dosing charts, mixing guides or claims about what the peptide does, points the other way.1

    Which shops have had letters?

    Our letters page lists them. A letter is the FDA's view at the time, not a court ruling; our guide What an FDA warning letter means explains what happens next.

    What should a buyer take from it?

    • The label tells you the product was not made, tested or approved for people. Read it as a warning, not as a loophole.
    • There is no dose on the box, no prescriber and no pharmacy behind it, and no one to call if something goes wrong.
    • A lab report, if there is one, covers one batch; our guide How to read a COA shows what it can and cannot tell you.

    For most peptides sold this way, such as BPC-157 and TB-500, there is no approved version at all. Each one's page under Peptides A to Z shows its FDA status, and our recovery page puts them next to the usual treatments.

    How do we show research-use shops?

    We list them so you can see the facts, never to sell. We do not link to any research-use shop, we take no money from them and they get no Paid link. Each one has a page with its five checks, and the seller windows on our goal pages show its prices next to the others.4

    Is it legal to buy?

    The FDA's letters go to sellers, not to people who buy for themselves. What the law means for you as a buyer is a legal question, and a lawyer can answer for your state. Our guide Are peptides legal in the US? explains the four kinds of peptide.

    None of this is legal or medical advice.
